_meta: Three complete candidate sequences from a decoder, each given as its per-token probabilities, used to show that beam search must normalize a hypothesis's score by its length -- otherwise it systematically prefers the shorter sequence, because every token multiplies in another probability below one and so subtracts another negative term from the log-probability. Beam search scores a partial or complete hypothesis by the product of its token probabilities, equivalently the sum of the token log-probabilities. That sum can only decrease as the sequence grows, since each log-probability is negative, so a short generic sequence beats a long fluent one on raw score even when the long one is more probable token for token. The result is the well-known length bias of beam search: raw beam collapses toward short, terse, often empty outputs. The fix is length normalization -- divide the summed log-probability by the sequence length (optionally length raised to a penalty exponent alpha) so the score is a per-token average rather than a total, which no longer shrinks just because there are more tokens. On this fixture the short candidate 'ok.' has a low per-token probability (0.45) but wins on raw sum because it is one token, while the long candidate has a high per-token probability (0.70) at every step yet loses on raw sum purely for being five tokens; length normalization reverses this and picks the fluent long sequence. candidates is the list; each candidate's label is a display string and token_probs is its per-token probabilities. The raw score, the per-token geometric mean, and the length-normalized score are computed.
